Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021): The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments. returnedRecords.text: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022): The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021): The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021): About $550 billion in new money for roads, bridges, water pipes, rural broadband and the electric grid, spread over five years. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022): The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. Still in effect; the under-21 provisions expire in 2032 by the law's own terms. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The CHIPS and Science Act (2022): About $52 billion to pay companies to build computer-chip factories in the United States, after the pandemic showed how much depends on chips made elsewhere. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Honoring our PACT Act (2022): Extended VA health care and disability benefits to veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic hazards, and made the government presume certain illnesses were service-related instead of making each veteran prove it. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Inflation Reduction Act (2022): Let Medicare negotiate the price of some prescription drugs and capped insulin at $35 a month for people on Medicare, alongside tax credits for clean energy, paid for partly by a minimum tax on large corporations. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Respect for Marriage Act (2022): Requires every state to recognize same-sex and interracial marriages performed in other states, so those marriages stay valid even if the Supreme Court changes course. returnedRecords.text: The Fiscal Responsibility Act (2023): Ended the debt-ceiling standoff by suspending the borrowing limit into 2025, in exchange for caps on federal spending and new work requirements for some food-stamp recipients. returnedRecords.text: En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021): The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021): About $550 billion in new money for roads, bridges, water pipes, rural broadband and the electric grid, spread over five years. returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022): The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. Still in effect; the under-21 provisions expire in 2032 by the law's own terms. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The CHIPS and Science Act (2022): About $52 billion to pay companies to build computer-chip factories in the United States, after the pandemic showed how much depends on chips made elsewhere. returnedRecords.text: The Honoring our PACT Act (2022): Extended VA health care and disability benefits to veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic hazards, and made the government presume certain illnesses were service-related instead of making each veteran prove it. returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021): The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021): About $550 billion in new money for roads, bridges, water pipes, rural broadband and the electric grid, spread over five years. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022): The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. Still in effect; the under-21 provisions expire in 2032 by the law's own terms. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The CHIPS and Science Act (2022): About $52 billion to pay companies to build computer-chip factories in the United States, after the pandemic showed how much depends on chips made elsewhere. returnedRecords.text: The Honoring our PACT Act (2022): Extended VA health care and disability benefits to veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic hazards, and made the government presume certain illnesses were service-related instead of making each veteran prove it. returnedRecords.text: The Inflation Reduction Act (2022): Let Medicare negotiate the price of some prescription drugs and capped insulin at $35 a month for people on Medicare, alongside tax credits for clean energy, paid for partly by a minimum tax on large corporations. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: The Respect for Marriage Act (2022): Requires every state to recognize same-sex and interracial marriages performed in other states, so those marriages stay valid even if the Supreme Court changes course. returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021): The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021): About $550 billion in new money for roads, bridges, water pipes, rural broadband and the electric grid, spread over five years. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022): The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. Still in effect; the under-21 provisions expire in 2032 by the law's own terms. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The CHIPS and Science Act (2022): About $52 billion to pay companies to build computer-chip factories in the United States, after the pandemic showed how much depends on chips made elsewhere. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Honoring our PACT Act (2022): Extended VA health care and disability benefits to veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic hazards, and made the government presume certain illnesses were service-related instead of making each veteran prove it. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: The Inflation Reduction Act (2022): Let Medicare negotiate the price of some prescription drugs and capped insulin at $35 a month for people on Medicare, alongside tax credits for clean energy, paid for partly by a minimum tax on large corporations. returnedRecords.text: The Respect for Marriage Act (2022): Requires every state to recognize same-sex and interracial marriages performed in other states, so those marriages stay valid even if the Supreme Court changes course. returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021): The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021): About $550 billion in new money for roads, bridges, water pipes, rural broadband and the electric grid, spread over five years. returnedRecords.text: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022): The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. Still in effect; the under-21 provisions expire in 2032 by the law's own terms. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.
returnedRecords.sourceOrg: congress.gov bill text and official summary

returnedRecords.text: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021): The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021): About $550 billion in new money for roads, bridges, water pipes, rural broadband and the electric grid, spread over five years. returnedRecords.text: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022): The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

request.question: What does Teri Ann Hourihan say about ARIZONA?

expectedRecords.quote: Teri Ann Hourihan ARIZONA GOVERNOR, NO LABELS PARTY I AM THE CANDIDATE THAT NO ONE ELSE IS OR IS WILLING TO BE — FOR THE PEOPLE = YOU.
I AM NOT FOR THE SYSTEM THAT FAILS US BUT FOR THE PEOPLE FIRST AND FOREMOST WHO ARE HURTING IN ARIZONA.

As Governor, my loyalty will be to the people of Arizona, not to special interests or big donors.” —Teri Ann Hourihan My Heart is For Arizona I rejected the No Labels Party endorsement because I stand for Arizona and not for a political party!
As Governor of Arizona, I will never take for granted the opportunity to serve the people of this great state.
My focus is simple: creating positive change, restoring accountability, and putting the people of Arizona first.
What I once saw as the darkest season of my life has become a calling to serve Arizona.
My goal is simple: improve the quality of life for every person who calls Arizona home.
November is ahead of us, and together we can save Arizona.
🙌🇺🇸 From the very beginning, I told Arizona, the media, my party, and everyone who would listen that I believe this campaign is a calling on my life.
Now it’s time for Arizona to recognize something important: we are not just a two-party state.
Get excited, Arizona!
As Governor of Arizona, I will not take corporate PAC money, billionaire donations, or special-interest endorsements.
My loyalty will be to the people of Arizona—not to those seeking favors, influence, or access.
Arizona deserves leadership that cannot be bought.
Together, we can build an Arizona that works for all of us Leading Arizona with Truth and Accountability Teri Ann Hourihan for AZ Governor .
Arizona has so much to lose if the wrong leader earns the Governor’s seat.
We can continue down the same path of division, waste, and failed leadership, or we can choose a new direction built on truth, accountability, and putting the people of Arizona first.
Arizona deserves better, and I’m ready to lead FRIENDSHIP AND GRATITUDE Teri Ann Hourihan for AZ Governor.

I regained my voice because his encouragement kept me speaking Q&A Affordability Arizona’s cost of living and inflation rates remain above national targets, making it increasingly difficult for families to afford housing, groceries, transportation, and other necessities.
Arizona’s rapid growth, combined with water shortages, drought conditions, and housing supply constraints, has driven costs higher.
Q&A Healthcare Healthcare costs continue to place a significant burden on Arizona families, employers, and healthcare providers.
Arizona can lead the nation in creating a healthcare system that supports families, employers, providers, and taxpayers while delivering better outcomes for everyone.
As Governor, I will fight for practical, fiscally responsible solutions that lower costs, expand choices, and make healthcare more affordable for every Arizona family.
Meet Teri Teri Ann Hourihan is a proud Arizona native, devoted mother, small business owner of an integrated health care company, and Licensed Professional Counselor (LPC).
Teri entered the race for Governor with one mission: to serve the people of Arizona.

Arizona deserves better.” — Teri Statement Teri chose to run as an Independent/No Labels because she believes the growing political division in our state and nation is preventing meaningful solutions and leaving too many people behind.
She believes Arizona needs leadership that brings people together, not further apart, and that the needs of citizens must always come before political agendas.

Guided by honesty, integrity, accountability, and common sense, Teri is committed to making decisions based on what is best for Arizona—not what is best for political parties, special interests, or wealthy donors.

She believes many of Arizona’s systems are no longer serving citizens as intended and that meaningful reform is necessary to protect families, strengthen communities, and improve quality of life across the state.
She is committed to being accessible, approachable, and accountable to the people of Arizona.
Teri’s Debate on 06/18/2026 Simply put, as Governor I will save Families and Save Arizona!
My mission is to create a government that is truly for the people and not for the government, to expose the truth, and to create a better Arizona for us all to live in.

returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.
